lessons.title: What ERP Is and Why Companies Use It
How Business Processes Flow Through an ERP

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real order-to-cash process (a customer orders a product, it is shipped, then invoiced and paid) and, without using any software, trace every step by hand across the departments that touch it -- Sales, Warehouse/Supply Chain, Finance -- writing down what information each department needs from the one before it. Then write a short paragraph explaining what breaks down in that same process if each department kept its own separate spreadsheet instead of sharing one ERP system.
slots.deliverable: A step-by-step order-to-cash process map (department by department) plus a short written explanation of the specific breakdowns a shared ERP system prevents.

lessons.title: Modules and Integration: Finance, Procurement, Supply Chain, HR
On-Premises ERP vs. Cloud ERP

slots.practicalActivity: List the four core Oracle module families (Financials, Procurement, Supply Chain Management, HCM) and, for each, name one piece of master data it shares with another module, matching the lesson's own examples (the supplier record shared between Procurement and Payables, the employee record shared between HCM and Expenses). Then search for one real company's public statement about moving from an on-premises ERP to a cloud ERP and summarize in 3-4 sentences what it cited as the business reason for switching.
slots.deliverable: A four-module master-data reference table, plus a short written summary of one real company's documented reason for migrating from on-premises to cloud ERP.

lessons.title: The Finance Department and Who Uses the System

slots.practicalActivity: Research the real organizational structure of a mid-size or large public company's finance department (using its investor-relations site, LinkedIn, or a published annual report) and map at least 5 roles you find there (for example AP Clerk, GL Accountant, Controller, CFO) to which Oracle Fusion module or work area each role would most likely use day to day, based on what Lesson 3 established about module ownership.
slots.deliverable: A 5-role finance-department-to-Oracle-module mapping table built from a real company's actual organizational structure.

lessons.title: What Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications Are
The SaaS Model and What Oracle Manages for You

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short two-column comparison, in your own words, of what Oracle manages for you under the SaaS model (infrastructure, patching, quarterly updates) versus what the customer still owns (configuration, data, security role assignments, user training). Then find Oracle's own public page describing Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications on oracle.com and list the specific application pillars it names.
slots.deliverable: A two-column SaaS responsibility table (Oracle vs. customer) plus a list of the application pillars taken from Oracle's own public site.

lessons.title: Oracle Fusion Cloud ERP vs. Oracle E-Business Suite
Oracle Fusion Cloud Architecture Overview

slots.practicalActivity: Build a side-by-side comparison table contrasting Oracle Fusion Cloud ERP and Oracle E-Business Suite across at least 4 dimensions (hosting/deployment, UI, upgrade cadence, customization approach), checking your answers against Oracle's own published EBS-to-Fusion comparison materials where you're unsure. Then sketch a simple boxes-and-arrows diagram showing how a Fusion Cloud customer's Production and non-production environments relate to each other.
slots.deliverable: A 4-dimension Fusion-vs-EBS comparison table and a diagram of Production/non-production environment relationships.

lessons.title: Quarterly Updates and Release Management

slots.practicalActivity: Search Oracle's own documentation for its real Fusion Cloud quarterly-update cadence and advance-notice window (for example, search 'Oracle Fusion Cloud quarterly update readiness' on oracle.com or Oracle Support), and write down the real facts you find. Then write a short release-management plan for a fictional company receiving its next quarterly update: who reviews the release notes first, what gets tested in non-production, and who signs off before it reaches Production.
slots.deliverable: Documented real Oracle quarterly-update cadence facts, plus a written release-management plan naming reviewers, test steps, and a sign-off owner.

lessons.title: Signing In and the Home Page
Navigating Oracle Fusion Cloud

slots.practicalActivity: Since hands-on Oracle Fusion access doesn't start until the Enterprise Structures & Chart of Accounts course (per Lesson 20), study 2-3 real Oracle Fusion Cloud home-page and Navigator screenshots from Oracle's own public documentation on docs.oracle.com (search 'Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications Getting Started'), and sketch your own labeled diagram contrasting the home page's springboard with the full Navigator menu, noting in your own words what 'simplified UI' means compared to older enterprise software like E-Business Suite.
slots.deliverable: A labeled home-page/Navigator diagram built from real Oracle documentation screenshots, plus a written explanation of 'simplified UI' in your own words.

lessons.title: Tasks, Work Areas and the Navigator
Searching, Favorites and Saved Searches

slots.practicalActivity: From the Oracle documentation screenshots gathered in the previous slot (or new ones for a specific work area, such as General Ledger or Payables), list 5 real work areas visible in the Navigator and the product family each belongs to (Financials, Procurement, Supply Chain, HCM). Then write a short plan naming which 3 work areas you would mark as Favorites on day one of a new Financials consultant role, and why.
slots.deliverable: A 5-work-area-to-product-family list sourced from real Oracle documentation, plus a justified 3-item Favorites plan for a new consultant.

lessons.title: Scheduled Processes and Job Monitoring
Environments: DEV, TEST and PROD

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the 5 scheduled-process job statuses (Pending, Running, Succeeded, Warning, Error) from memory, then write a 3-step troubleshooting script for the lesson's own support scenario -- 'my report never showed up' -- naming exactly what you would check in the Scheduled Processes work area before escalating. Then write a short explanation of why an environment refresh (copying Production's data into non-production) can wipe out in-progress configuration work, and what an implementation team should do to protect against that.
slots.deliverable: A written 5-status job reference, a 3-step troubleshooting script for a missing-report ticket, and a short written explanation of the environment-refresh risk and mitigation.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for Working in Oracle Fusion: write a single realistic new-hire scenario where you (a) sign in and locate 3 specific real work areas through the Navigator, citing the screenshots or documentation you used, (b) mark one as a Favorite and explain why, (c) submit and monitor a scheduled process through all 5 statuses in your written walkthrough, and (d) explain which environment -- Production or non-production -- each action would actually happen in and why, tying in the quarterly-update testing point from Lesson 10.
slots.deliverable: One written end-to-end new-hire navigation walkthrough combining the Navigator, Favorites, scheduled-process monitoring, and environment awareness from this chapter.

lessons.title: Implementation Terminology You Will Hear
Offerings, Functional Areas and Setup and Maintenance

slots.practicalActivity: Build a glossary of at least 8 implementation terms from the lesson (for example offering, functional area, fit-gap, CRP, go-live) with your own one-sentence definition for each. Then describe, in your own words, how the Setup and Maintenance work area organizes configuration into offerings and functional areas, using the Financials offering as your worked example.
slots.deliverable: An 8-term implementation-vocabulary glossary with original definitions, plus a written explanation of how Setup and Maintenance organizes the Financials offering.

lessons.title: Functional vs. Technical Oracle Careers
Your Practice Environment: What It Is and When to Activate It

slots.practicalActivity: Write a two-paragraph self-assessment: which side of the functional-vs-technical consultant split fits your own background and interests better, and why, naming at least 2 specific day-to-day tasks from each side the lesson described (fit-gap sessions and Chart of Accounts design for functional; FBDI data loads and REST API integrations for technical). Then write down, in your own planner, the exact course on this path -- Enterprise Structures & Chart of Accounts -- where you will activate your paid Oracle practice-instance subscription, and explain in one sentence why activating it now, during this course, would waste paid access time.
slots.deliverable: A written functional-vs-technical self-assessment with specific day-to-day task references, plus a noted activation plan naming the correct future course for starting the practice-environment subscription.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can explain what Oracle Fusion Cloud ERP is and how it differs from on-premises ERP and E-Business Suite, describe how to navigate its home page, Navigator, and Scheduled Processes work area conceptually, and decide whether the functional or technical consultant track fits them before spending a dollar on hands-on practice access.
